meaning.rapid_rise: The lake is noticeably larger than in previous years. For proglacial and moraine lakes this usually reflects glacier retreat and meltwater inflow. Growth alone does not mean the lake will burst, but such lakes deserve more frequent observation and expert attention.
meaning.rising: The lake area is gradually increasing. This is a reason to watch the lake more closely, not a sign of immediate danger.
meaning.new_lake: A new lake has formed here. Young lakes on moraines and near glaciers can change quickly, so they are worth watching from their first years.
meaning.stable: No notable change: the lake area stays close to its long-term normal.
meaning.falling: The lake is smaller than usual. Possible causes are drainage, seepage through the moraine, or less meltwater inflow.
meaning.insufficient_data: There is too little data to draw conclusions yet.
hero.title: What is happening to the mountain lakes above Almaty
hero.lead: The glaciers of Ile Alatau are retreating, and lakes are forming and growing at their edges. We measure the area of these lakes from satellite images and show where the water level is rising.

risk.title: Why the lakes are dangerous
risk.p1: As a glacier retreats, meltwater collects in front of it and on the moraine — the ridge of rock and ice the glacier leaves behind. This is how proglacial and moraine lakes form.
risk.p2: A moraine is an unreliable dam: it contains ice that is also melting. If water overtops the rim or finds a way through the moraine, the lake can empty within hours. The flood picks up rock and soil and becomes a mudflow.
risk.p3: The danger depends not only on the size of a lake but on where its water goes. That is why we show a computed flow path for every lake and the town that lies downstream.
history.1963: A catastrophic mudflow in the Issyk river valley.
history.1973: On 15 July a moraine lake below Tuyuksu Glacier burst in the upper Malaya Almatinka valley, at about 3,400 m. The lake held an estimated 220,000 m³. The mudflow was stopped by the Medeu dam, completed shortly before.

method.title: How it works
method.p1: The European Space Agency's Sentinel-2 satellites image every point on Earth every 2–5 days at 10-metre resolution. The images are free and open.
method.p2: For each lake we take all summer images (July–September, when lakes are ice-free) since 2019 and compute the water index NDWI = (Green − NIR) / (Green + NIR). Water absorbs near-infrared light, so water has an index above zero while rock and grass are below. A pixel with NDWI above {threshold} is counted as water.
method.p3: Images with more than {clouds}% cloud or {snow}% snow over the lake are discarded. The season area is the median of all usable images; the normal is the median of all previous years for the same months.
method.p4: Limitations: an optical satellite cannot see through clouds; small lakes are only dozens of pixels; area is only an indirect indicator of water volume. So the site shows signals worth an expert's attention, not an outburst forecast.
method.statuses: “Rapid growth”: the season area is at least 30% and at least 3,000 m² above the long-term normal, and also above the maximum of all previous years. “Growing”: at least 12% and 2,000 m² above normal, or steady growth over several years. “Shrinking”: at least 15% and 2,000 m² below normal. “New lake”: there was almost no water here when observations began. The square-metre thresholds keep measurement noise on small lakes from looking like an alarm.
about.title: About
about.p1: In the Ile Alatau mountains above Almaty there are moraine and proglacial lakes. As glaciers retreat these lakes grow, and an outburst can trigger a mudflow. LakeWatch is an open project that tracks the area of these lakes from satellite images and makes the data available to everyone.
about.p2: The code and data are open. Measurements for each lake can be downloaded as CSV.
disclaimer: This is an open research project, not an official warning system. Official information on mudflow hazards comes from the Ministry of Emergency Situations of Kazakhstan and Kazselezashchita. Emergency number: 112.
footer.data: Data: Copernicus Sentinel-2 (ESA), Microsoft Planetary Computer, OpenStreetMap. Basemap: Esri World Imagery.

mud.title: Mudflows that have already happened
mud.lead: Six events over a century that led Almaty to build dams and learn to warn people in time. Four of them began with a mountain lake bursting — exactly the kind of lake this site watches.
mud.note: Figures come from the sources listed. Where sources disagree, we say so. The exact death toll of the older disasters is still unknown.
mud.lesson.title: What this tells us
mud.lesson.text: The danger is usually visible in advance: a lake grows for years before it bursts. In 1973 the city was saved by a dam built beforehand and a warning issued two days earlier. That is why watching the lakes every year matters as much as building defences.
mud.1921.title: The Verny disaster
mud.1921.place: Malaya Almatinka river, the town of Verny (now Almaty)
mud.1921.cause: A heavy downpour in the mountains. The Shymbulak river basin is considered the main source of the flow.
mud.1921.course: The flow ran down the Malaya Almatinka, and part of it turned into what is now Kunaev Street. Within a few hours a large part of the town was destroyed and buried under mud and rock.
mud.1921.damage: About 500 deaths is the figure most often cited, in a town of roughly 45,000 people. The exact number is unknown.
mud.1963.title: The loss of Lake Issyk
mud.1963.place: Lake Issyk, about 45 km east of Almaty
mud.1963.cause: Meltwater from the Zharsai glacier overfilled the mountain lake Zharsai, which broke through its natural barrier.
mud.1963.course: The flow crashed into Lake Issyk and washed out its natural dam. Within hours the lake had almost vanished, and the mudflow reached the town of Issyk.
mud.1963.damage: Homes, a hydropower plant and a winery were destroyed. It was a day off and many people were at the lake; soldiers evacuated about 2,000 of them. The exact death toll is still unknown.
mud.1973.title: The mudflow stopped by the Medeu dam
mud.1973.cause: At about 3,400 m a moraine lake below the Tuyuksu glacier burst. It held about 220,000 m³ of water.
mud.1973.course: The outburst flood destroyed the gabion dam at Mynzhylky and turned into a mudflow. Estimates of its volume range from 3.8 to 5.3 million m³.
mud.1973.damage: The Medeu dam, completed shortly before, held the flow back and the city was not harmed. Kazhydromet issued a mudflow warning on 13 July, two days earlier. The dam was raised after the event.
mud.1977.title: A month of mudflows on the Bolshaya Almatinka
mud.1977.place: The Kumbel river and the Bolshaya Almatinka valley
mud.1977.cause: Lake No. 13 by the Sovetov glacier burst. It was being drained artificially, and the temporary dam of sandbags gave way: more than 88,000 m³ of water escaped in 20 minutes.
mud.1977.course: Mudflows kept coming for almost a month: specialists counted about 400 surges, some 10–12 m high. The total volume is estimated at about 6 million m³ — one of the largest glacial mudflows in Ile Alatau.
mud.1977.damage: The sources we found give no information about casualties.
mud.2015.title: The Kargalinka mudflow
mud.2015.place: The Kargalinka river, Nauryzbay district of Almaty
mud.2015.cause: According to Kazselezashchita, a moraine lake burst at about 2:15 a.m., releasing about 40,000 m³ of water. It followed a spell of abnormal heat.
mud.2015.course: The flow flooded the settlements of Kargaly and Karagaily and washed out roads.
mud.2015.damage: About 97 houses were flooded and up to 900 people were evacuated. No one died. Residents received the SMS warning only several hours later.
mud.2024.title: The Shymbulak mudflow
mud.2024.place: The Left Shymbulak river basin, Shymbulak resort
mud.2024.cause: A heavy downpour. According to Kazhydromet scientists, the slopes had been weakened because the soil and vegetation were disturbed when ski runs were graded about 11 years earlier.
mud.2024.course: The mudflow formed during intense rain while air temperatures were high.
mud.2024.damage: Scientists described this mudflow as anthropogenic, meaning it was caused in part by human activity.
